architecture_basis.decision: Broad angle relationships is reporting-only ALL_OF; complement, supplement, vertical equality and supplied-total adjacent-angle addition require distinct evidence. Expected count is distinct from experimental frequency.

standards_context.note: Expectation references are provenance for the authoring request, not accepted standards mappings.

constraints: Eight unchanged r1/r2 cards have mathematical-scope approval; the three corrected r3 cards remain pending limited independent review.
No proposed code is authoritative until Architecture confirms identity and Independent Mathematical Review approves scope.
Existing broad canonical identities, local seed identifiers, UUIDs, variants and learner evidence remain unchanged.
Generator availability is overlap evidence only and is not mathematical proof, standards coverage, assessment readiness or mastery evidence.
Production TAXONOMY remains unchanged and empty.
M8.G.TRANS and M8.G.SIM are deferred until authoritative Integrated Algebra I/II scope reconciliation; no historical evidence is reinterpreted.

cards.name: Reason with circle circumference
cards.scope: Use C=2πr=πd to determine or interpret the circumference of a circle from radius, diameter, or a one-step inverse condition, with units and requested exact or approximate form.
inclusions: Positive rational radius or diameter
Exact answers in terms of π when requested
Decimal approximations only to a stated precision
One-step inverse cases such as C=10π implies d=10
Contextual interpretation as distance around a circle
exclusions: Arbitrary symbolic manipulation beyond one-step inversion
Treating a decimal approximation of π as exact
Inferring mastery from radius-diameter conversion alone
prerequisites: meaning of π as circumference-to-diameter ratio

examples.prompt: A circle has radius 7 cm. Give its circumference exactly.
A circle has circumference 10π m. Find its diameter.
A circle has diameter 8 cm. Give its circumference to the nearest tenth using π≈3.14159.
A circle has radius 5 cm. Its circumference is 25π cm.
examples.rationale: 25π is the area, not the circumference

misconceptions: uses πr² for circumference
uses radius as diameter or diameter as radius
drops linear units
reports 3.14-based value as exact
assessment_criteria: independent evidence from both radius and diameter
at least one exact-π and one stated-precision response
at least one contextual interpretation with linear units
separate direct and inverse evidence
do not infer area mastery

cards.name: Reason with circle area
cards.scope: Use A=πr² to determine or interpret the area of a circle from radius or diameter, and solve bounded one-step inverse cases where A/π is a perfect square, with correct square units and requested exact or approximate form.
inclusions: Positive rational radius or diameter
Radius extraction from a supplied diameter
Exact answers in terms of π
Stated-precision approximations
Inverse cases whose radius is rational and evident from a perfect-square quotient
exclusions: Surface area of cylinders or spheres

examples.prompt: A circle has radius 6 cm. Give its area exactly.
A circle has diameter 10 m. Give its area exactly.
A circle has area 49π cm². Find its radius.
A circle has radius 4 cm. Its area is 8π cm².

misconceptions: uses 2πr for area
fails to halve a diameter before squaring
squares π as well as the radius
uses linear rather than square units
assessment_criteria: independent radius and diameter cases
exact-π and stated-precision evidence
at least one square-unit interpretation
one bounded inverse case
do not infer circumference mastery

cards.name: Reason with complementary angles
possible_overlaps: unconfirmed historical or persisted spelling MATH.GEO.ANGLE.COMPLEMENT
cards.scope: Identify and use the fact that two complementary angles have measures summing to 90° to determine an unknown positive angle measure and justify the equation used.
inclusions: Positive whole-number and rational degree measures strictly between 0° and 90°
Diagram and diagram-independent verbal cases
One- and two-step linear equations whose geometrically valid solution gives complementary constituent angles
Verification that the two measures sum to 90°
exclusions: Adjacent-angle addition without a supplied 90° total
Treating a generator-family literal as canonical identity authority
prerequisites: addition and subtraction of rational numbers

examples.prompt: Two angles are complementary. One measures 37°. Find the other.
Complementary angles measure (2x+10)° and 40°. Find x.
Angles measuring 50° and 50° are complementary.

misconceptions: uses 180° instead of 90°
assumes adjacency alone makes angles complementary
accepts zero or negative constituent angles
reverses the unknown-angle subtraction
assessment_criteria: independent numeric and algebraic complementary-angle evidence
include a diagram-independent verbal case and a diagram case
require an equation or justification using a 90° total
include a validity or misconception probe
do not infer supplementary, vertical, adjacent-addition or triangle-angle mastery

cards.name: Reason with supplementary angles
possible_overlaps: unconfirmed historical or persisted spelling MATH.GEO.ANGLE.SUPPLEMENT
cards.scope: Identify and use the fact that two supplementary angles have measures summing to 180° to determine an unknown positive angle measure and justify the equation used; a linear pair is an included geometric context, not a separate identity.
inclusions: Positive whole-number and rational degree measures strictly between 0° and 180°
Linear-pair and nonadjacent supplementary contexts
One- and two-step linear equations whose geometrically valid solution gives supplementary constituent angles
Verification that the two measures sum to 180°
exclusions: Assuming every adjacent pair is supplementary
Treating linear-pair context as a second mastery credit
prerequisites: addition and subtraction of rational numbers

examples.prompt: Two angles form a linear pair. One measures 68°. Find the other.
Supplementary angles measure (3x+5)° and 80°. Find x.
Two adjacent angles measure 70° and 80°, so they are supplementary.
examples.rationale: Adjacency alone does not establish a 180° total, and these measures sum to 150°

misconceptions: uses 90° instead of 180°
treats all adjacent angles as supplementary
uses 360° for a linear pair
awards separate credit for the same linear-pair evidence
assessment_criteria: independent numeric and algebraic supplementary-angle evidence
include both a linear-pair context and a nonadjacent stated-supplement context
require an equation or justification using a 180° total
include an adjacency-alone rejection probe
do not infer complement, vertical, adjacent-addition or triangle-angle mastery

cards.name: Reason with vertical-angle equality
possible_overlaps: generator implementations that include vertical angles
cards.scope: Identify opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines as vertical angles, use their equality to determine unknown positive angle measures, and justify the equality from the intersection structure.
inclusions: Whole-number and rational degree measures strictly between 0° and 180°
Numeric and one- or two-step algebraic unknowns
Selecting the opposite nonadjacent pair at an intersection
Verification that vertical angles have equal measures
exclusions: Assuming visually similar angles are vertical without intersection structure

examples.prompt: Opposite angles formed by intersecting lines measure (3x+5)° and 80°. Find x.
At an intersection, one angle is 47°. Find its vertical angle.
Two adjacent angles at an intersection are vertical angles.
examples.rationale: Vertical angles are opposite and nonadjacent

misconceptions: confuses vertical with adjacent angles
assumes every equal-looking pair is vertical
uses a 180° sum instead of equality for the opposite pair
accepts a nonpositive or straight constituent angle
assessment_criteria: independent numeric and algebraic vertical-angle evidence
require identification of the opposite nonadjacent pair
require an equality-based equation or justification
include a vertical-versus-adjacent misconception probe
do not infer supplementary, adjacent-addition or triangle-angle mastery

cards.name: Reason with adjacent-angle addition
cards.scope: Use addition of nonoverlapping adjacent angle measures in either explicit part-whole structure: the whole is supplied and a part is missing, or every constituent part is supplied and the whole is missing; adjacency alone supplies no numerical total.
inclusions: Positive whole-number and rational constituent measures
A supplied whole or total with one constituent part missing
All nonoverlapping constituent parts supplied with the whole angle missing
Numeric missing-part, missing-whole, and bounded one- or two-step algebraic cases
Verification that the adjacent nonoverlapping parts sum to the whole
exclusions: Inferring a 90°, 180°, or 360° total from adjacency alone
Complementary or supplementary credit unless that total is explicitly part of the primary item
Multiple mastery credits from one primary attempt
prerequisites: addition and subtraction of rational numbers

examples.prompt: Adjacent angles partition an 85° angle. One part is 32°. Find the other.
Adjacent angles measure (x+12)° and 28° and together form a 70° angle. Find x.
Two nonoverlapping adjacent angles measure 32° and 53°. Find the measure of the whole angle they form.
Two adjacent angles measure 30° and 40°, so their total must be 90°.
examples.rationale: Adjacency alone supplies no fixed total; the two stated measures sum to 70°

misconceptions: assumes adjacent angles are automatically complementary
assumes adjacent angles are automatically supplementary
double-counts an overlapping region
subtracts from an unstated conventional total
assessment_criteria: independent missing-part evidence with an explicitly supplied whole or total
independent missing-whole evidence with all nonoverlapping constituent parts supplied
include numeric and algebraic cases
require an addition equation or part-whole justification
include an adjacency-alone no-total rejection probe
one primary atom per attempt; do not award complement, supplement or reporting-profile credit from the same evidence

cards.name: Reason with triangle interior and exterior angles
cards.scope: Use the 180° interior-angle sum and the exterior-angle theorem to determine unknown triangle angle measures, test geometric validity, and justify relationships.
inclusions: Missing interior angles
Exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles
Linear-pair connection at a triangle vertex
Whole-number and rational degree measures
Rejecting nonpositive or impossible angle sets
exclusions: Assuming a diagram is drawn to scale
prerequisites: addition and subtraction of rational numbers

examples.prompt: A triangle has angles 48° and 67°. Find the third angle.
A triangle has remote interior angles 42° and 73°. Find the adjacent exterior angle.
A triangle has angles 90°, 60°, and 40°.

misconceptions: uses 360° as a triangle interior sum
adds the adjacent interior angle to remote interior angles for the exterior theorem
trusts visual scale over stated measures
accepts zero or negative angles
assessment_criteria: separate interior-sum and exterior-angle evidence
at least one validity/rejection probe
require a theorem-based equation or explanation
do not infer congruence, similarity, or side-length reasoning

cards.name: Quantify event likelihood from 0 to 1
cards.scope: Within a finite discrete probability model in which every elementary outcome has positive probability, represent and interpret event likelihood on the inclusive scale from 0 to 1; probability 0 identifies an impossible event, probability 1 identifies a certain event, and intermediate values compare relative likelihood.
inclusions: Finite discrete probability models whose elementary outcomes all have positive probability
Fraction and decimal probability representations in the inclusive interval [0,1]
Percent probability representations from 0% to 100% inclusive
Conversion among equivalent fraction, decimal, and percent representations
Ordering and comparing likelihoods
Impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, and certain interpretations within the bounded finite-discrete model
For one event and its complement, p=0.5 means the two are equally likely; distinct events can have equal probability at values other than 0.5
exclusions: Computing experimental relative frequency from data
Continuous or general probability spaces where a probability-zero event need not be impossible
Claiming that a likely event must occur
prerequisites: fractions, decimals, and percents as equivalent representations

examples.prompt: Place probabilities 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, and 1 from impossible to certain.
In the finite sample space for one fair six-sided die, what is the probability of rolling 7?
examples.answer: 0; the event is impossible in this model.

examples.prompt: In the finite sample space for one fair six-sided die, what is the probability of rolling a number from 1 through 6?
examples.answer: 1; the event is certain in this model.

examples.prompt: Express 1/4 as a decimal and percent probability.
An event has probability 0.5. Compare the event with its complement.
Two distinct events each have probability 0.3. Can they be equally likely?
A probability is 120%.
examples.rationale: Percent probability must lie from 0% to 100% inclusive

misconceptions: treats probability 0.7 as 7 percent
believes likely means guaranteed
orders fractions by denominator alone
accepts fractions or decimals outside [0,1] or percents outside 0%..100%
claims that two distinct events can be equally likely only when both have probability 0.5
applies the finite-discrete 0/impossible converse to an excluded continuous probability model
assessment_criteria: include finite-discrete event-model evidence for probability 0 as impossible and probability 1 as certain
include percent boundaries 0% and 100%
require observable fraction-decimal-percent equivalence evidence
compare and order multiple representations
distinguish event-versus-complement equality at p=0.5 from equal probability of two distinct events
require interpretation as well as representation
do not infer experimental-frequency or compound-event mastery

cards.name: Estimate probability using long-run relative frequency
cards.scope: Compute and interpret experimental probability as successes divided by trials, and reason qualitatively that relative frequency tends to stabilize near an underlying probability over many independent repeated trials conducted under unchanged conditions with a constant event probability, without requiring exact agreement.
inclusions: Finite independent repeated trials under unchanged conditions with constant event probability
Clearly identified event counts and total trial counts
Relative frequency as a fraction, decimal, or percent
Comparing results from different trial counts
Qualitative long-run stabilization under the stated stable repeated-trial model
Recognizing that finite experimental frequency need not equal a theoretical probability exactly
exclusions: Expected-count prediction using n×p as mastery evidence
Treating predicted or expected count as guaranteed
Formal confidence intervals or hypothesis tests
Replacing a theoretical model solely because one finite experiment differs

examples.prompt: A spinner lands blue 18 times in 30 trials. Find the experimental probability.
A fair coin gives 47 heads in 100 flips. Does this disprove probability 1/2?
A spinner is changed after 50 trials, then 50 more trials are combined with the first results. May the combined frequency be treated as stabilizing to one unchanged underlying probability?
examples.answer: not without a model that accounts for the changed conditions

examples.prompt: An event with probability 0.3 will occur exactly 30 times in 100 trials.
examples.rationale: 30 is an expectation, not a guarantee

misconceptions: reverses successes and trials
uses raw count instead of relative frequency when trial totals differ
expects exact theoretical frequency in every sample
treats more trials as making all outcomes identical
expects stabilization to one unchanged probability when conditions change or trials are dependent or adaptive
assessment_criteria: independent computation and interpretation evidence
compare samples with different totals using relative rather than raw frequency
include a long-run qualitative explanation under independent unchanged-condition trials with constant event probability
include a changed-condition or dependent/adaptive-trial probe that rejects unjustified stabilization
include expected-count-versus-guarantee only as a non-credit misconception contrast
do not award or infer expected-count mastery
do not infer formal statistical inference

cards.name: Compare theoretical and experimental probability models
cards.scope: Compare a stated theoretical probability model with experimental relative-frequency evidence, explain plausible random variation, and identify when persistent discrepancies justify questioning assumptions or model fit.
inclusions: Calculate both theoretical and experimental probabilities
Compare using common representations
Explain finite-sample variation
Recognize that larger repeated samples generally provide more stable evidence
Identify structural reasons a model may be inappropriate when supplied
exclusions: Automatically rejecting a model after any mismatch
Assuming experimental data proves exact theoretical probability

examples.prompt: A model predicts 1/2; an event occurs 52 times in 100 trials. Is the result necessarily inconsistent?
examples.answer: no; the difference can be random variation

examples.prompt: A supposedly fair die shows 6 on 240 of 300 trials. What should be questioned?
Experimental probability differs from theory, so theory is always wrong.

misconceptions: expects exact equality in finite trials
replaces theory with one observed proportion
ignores sample size
compares raw counts with unequal trial totals
assessment_criteria: compute or identify both model and observed proportion
include one plausible-variation case and one clear model-mismatch case
require explanation referencing sample size or assumptions
do not infer formal statistical-test mastery

cards.name: Represent sample spaces and probabilities for compound events
cards.scope: Construct and use an organized sample space for a finite two-stage experiment to determine probabilities of compound events, distinguishing ordered outcomes and updating outcome counts when dependence is explicitly described.
inclusions: Organized lists, tables, and tree diagrams
Two-stage experiments with equally likely elementary outcomes
AND and OR event descriptions in ordinary language
Complement of an event
With-replacement cases and explicitly bounded without-replacement cases
Probability as favorable elementary outcomes over total equally likely outcomes
exclusions: Assuming stages are independent without evidence
Three or more stages unless separately reviewed
Counting unordered pairs when order changes the outcome

examples.prompt: Flip a coin twice. List the ordered sample space.
Roll a fair die and flip a fair coin. Find P(even and heads).
When drawing without replacement, use the same denominator on the second draw.
HT and TH are the same ordered outcome.
examples.rationale: They differ when trial order is recorded

misconceptions: adds probabilities for an AND event without justification
multiplies dependent stages as though unchanged
omits ordered outcomes
counts favorable outcomes over a non-equally-likely list
assessment_criteria: construct an explicit sample space in at least two representations
separate independent and explicitly dependent cases
include AND, OR, and complement evidence
require denominator justification from elementary outcomes
do not infer general conditional probability

No evidence propagation or duplicate credit
